bank.q: You need to correct a colleague mid-sentence in a meeting. Which is the least abrupt?
bank.a: Can I just come in on that point?

bank.q: Someone has clearly said something they regret. Which reply eases the moment?

bank.q: You are describing your own history with letter-writing. Which sentence sounds most natural?

bank.q: Which opening suits an email to somebody you have never contacted before?
bank.a: I am writing to ask about the archive collection.
d: Hi — quick question about the archive.
Just wondering about the archive, thanks.

bank.q: A colleague argues that handwriting is finished. Which reply disagrees without dismissing them?
bank.a: Up to a point — though people still write by hand when it matters.
d: That is simply not true at all.

bank.q: You meet an unknown word in a text. What is the most efficient first step?
bank.a: decide from the sentence whether it is a thing, an action or a quality

bank.q: You must interrupt a caller to take another call. Which is best?

One second, do not go away.

bank.q: Which closing suits an informal email giving news to a friend?
bank.a: Anyway, that is my news — write and tell me yours.
d: I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully.
Please respond at your earliest convenience.
Thank you for your attention to this matter.

bank.q: Which sentence expresses permission rather than obligation?
bank.a: You can leave your bag at the desk.
d: You have to leave your bag at the desk.
You must leave your bag at the desk.
You are not allowed to leave your bag.

bank.q: You disagree that somebody who finds money should keep it. Which states the case most strongly but politely?
bank.a: I take the point about finders, but the owner's claim has to come first.
d: That is a ridiculous thing to think.
Nobody sensible would agree with you.

bank.q: Which notice expresses prohibition rather than advice?
bank.a: Items may not be removed from this room.
d: Items should be returned to the shelf.
Please take care of the items.
You are advised not to remove items.

bank.q: Which sentence draws a conclusion from evidence rather than stating a fact?
bank.a: Judging by the empty car park, the shift must have finished early.
d: The shift finishes early on Fridays.

bank.q: Which opening suits a persuasive letter to a council?
bank.a: I am writing to object to the proposed charge, for three reasons.
d: I really hate this new charge idea.
Why has nobody asked the residents?
This letter is about the parking charge.

bank.a: The revenue argument is a fair one, but it does not answer the main objection.
d: The revenue argument is completely wrong.
There is no revenue argument at all.
I will ignore the revenue argument.

bank.q: You are describing a trip that changed how you saw yourself. Which opening is most engaging?
bank.a: I had never slept outdoors in my life, and I had agreed to eleven nights of it.
d: I went on a trip and it was very good.

bank.q: You are telling a story and want to fill in something that happened earlier. Which signals that?
